items: Trace the lineage from symbiosis to tool-using agents
Name the recurring failure mode across sixty years

reading.text: Part VIII is the centre of gravity of this book, and it opens with history for a reason: almost every design problem in current AI products has a recognisable ancestor, and the ancestors mostly failed in ways that were diagnosed at the time.
The lineage

items: Licklider's symbiosis (1960) — humans set goals, machines do the routinisable work in between
ELIZA (Weizenbaum 1966), and Weizenbaum's own alarm at users' attachment in Computer Power and Human Reason (1976): the first anthropomorphism warning
Expert systems and their explanation facilities — MYCIN's ability to answer "why are you asking me this?" is XAI's ancestor
Programming by demonstration (Cypher, Watch What I Do, 1993)
Adaptive interfaces and the Clippy postmortem — intrusiveness plus poor modelling of interruption cost, under-implementing the Lumière research behind it
Recommender systems (GroupLens, Resnick et al., CSCW 1994)
Siri and Alexa (2011–14), deep-learning perception, LLM chat (2022), tool-using agents (2024–26)

reading.text: Weizenbaum's warning

Weizenbaum's alarm was not that ELIZA was clever. By his own account in Computer Power and Human Reason, his secretary — who had watched him build it — asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it privately. The attachment formed anyway, to a program written to show there was nothing there.

That episode is the earliest documented instance of what Reeves and Nass later formalised: the social response does not require belief, and knowing exactly how the mechanism works does not prevent it. It is worth sitting with, because every argument that users will not over-attribute understanding to a system once they understand it is an argument this anecdote already answered in 1966.
Clippy, and what it got wrong

The Clippy postmortem is the most instructive failure in the list because the research existed and the product did not implement it. The underlying Lumière work modelled user goals probabilistically and reasoned about when assistance was worth offering; the shipped assistant intervened on shallow triggers, without weighing the cost of interrupting. It was not that the idea was wrong — it was that the expected-utility calculation was skipped.
The recurring failure mode across sixty years: systems that take initiative without modelling the cost of being wrong about user intent.

Read the lineage with that sentence in hand and it organises the whole list. The adaptive interfaces that reorganised themselves, the assistant that offered help you did not want, the agent that refactored a file you did not mention — each acted on an inference about intent, and each failed to weigh what an incorrect inference would cost. Accuracy was never the missing piece; the cost model was.
That is why chapter 28 opens with Horvitz. The mixed-initiative principles are precisely a formalisation of the calculation these systems skipped, and they were published in 1999.

items: Licklider, Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960)
Weizenbaum, ELIZA (1966, CACM) and Computer Power and Human Reason (1976)
Cypher, Watch What I Do (1993)
Maes, Agents that Reduce Work and Information Overload (CACM 1994)
Resnick et al., GroupLens (CSCW 1994)
Shneiderman & Maes (1997, Interactions)

cards.back: Systems that take initiative without modelling the cost of being wrong about the user's intent.
Intrusiveness plus poor modelling of interruption cost — it under-implemented the Lumière research on when assistance is actually worth offering.
The explanation facilities of expert systems — MYCIN's ability to answer "why are you asking me this?"
That people formed real attachments to ELIZA despite knowing what it was — the first documented anthropomorphism alarm, from the system's own author.

quiz.question: What single flaw does the book identify across Clippy, early adaptive interfaces and current agents?
options: Taking initiative without modelling the cost of being wrong about intent
quiz.why: Accuracy is not the issue; the expected cost of an unwanted intervention is. This is exactly what Horvitz's mixed-initiative principles formalise.

quiz.question: Weizenbaum's concern about ELIZA was primarily that:
options: The program could pass for human indefinitely
People attached to it even knowing it was trivial
Its pattern matching was too crude to be useful
quiz.why: The attachment persisted despite full knowledge of the mechanism — which is why the Media Equation later formalised social response as automatic.

items: Apply Horvitz's expected-utility test to "ask or act?"
Place a product on the levels-of-automation scale
Recognise oversight theatre

reading.text: Every agent product answers one question repeatedly, usually without noticing: should the system act now, or stop and ask? This chapter contains the best available formalisation of that question, published in 1999, and a set of frameworks for describing how much autonomy a system actually has.
Horvitz's principles

Horvitz, "Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces" (CHI 1999): act when the expected utility of acting exceeds the expected utility of not acting, given uncertainty about the user's goals and the cost of interrupting them. Provide efficient invocation and dismissal, and maintain a dialogue over uncertain intentions.

The decisive move is treating the decision as expected utility rather than as a confidence threshold. Confidence is only one input: the others are what a correct action is worth, what an incorrect one costs, and what interrupting costs at this moment. A system can be highly confident and still be wrong to act, if being wrong is catastrophic or irreversible.

That framing dissolves a common design argument. "The model is 90% accurate, so it should just do it" is incomplete — 90% accuracy on an action that deletes work is a different proposition from 90% accuracy on an action that reorders a list. The threshold is not a property of the model; it is a property of the model crossed with the consequence.

Efficient invocation and dismissal is the underrated half of the paper. If the user can summon assistance cheaply and wave it away cheaply, the cost of the system guessing wrong falls, which in turn licenses it to guess more often. Much of what makes an assistant tolerable is not accuracy but the low cost of ignoring it.
How much autonomy is this, exactly?

Levels of automation (Sheridan & Verplank 1978; Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens 2000, IEEE SMC): a ten-level scale from fully manual to fully autonomous, applied separately to each information-processing stage — acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation.

The per-stage refinement is what makes the framework useful rather than a slogan. A system can gather information automatically, analyse it automatically, and still leave both the decision and the action to the human — or automate the decision and leave the action, which is what an approval gate is. Describing a product as "semi-autonomous" says almost nothing; saying which stages are automated says a great deal.
Modern agent products are levels-of-automation sliders whether their designers know it or not. Naming the stages makes the choice deliberate instead of emergent.

Shneiderman's HCAI framework (2020, 2022): high human control and high automation are compatible axes rather than endpoints of a single tradeoff. The target is the reliable, safe and trustworthy quadrant.

The reframing matters because the one-dimensional version smuggles in a false choice — that any increase in automation must cost control. Shneiderman's two-axis picture makes the high-high quadrant a design goal: systems that do a great deal and remain comprehensible and steerable. A car with power steering and anti-lock brakes is highly automated and highly controlled at once.
Oversight, and its counterfeit

Contemporary oversight design: approval gates scaled to reversibility, plan-then-execute disclosure, sandboxing and dry runs, and audit trails. The empirical thread at CHI and CSCW is unflattering — humans rubber-stamp agent plans under time pressure.

Each technique targets a different part of the problem. Scaling the gate to reversibility spends the user's attention where it can still change something. Plan-then-execute makes the intention inspectable before it becomes an action. Sandboxes and dry runs shrink the blast radius so that being wrong is survivable. Audit trails accept that some things will happen unwatched and make them reconstructable afterwards.
Approval UI without genuine evaluability is oversight theatre. If the reviewer cannot actually tell whether the plan is right, the approval step is not adding safety — it is transferring liability.

That is Bainbridge's irony wearing a modern interface. The human is placed in a monitoring role over a system that is usually correct, given a review artefact they have no realistic way to evaluate under time pressure, and then held responsible for the outcome. The design question is not whether there is an approval step but whether the step is capable of catching anything.

items: Horvitz, Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces (CHI 1999, DOI 10.1145/302979.303030)
Sheridan & Verplank (1978)
Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens, Types and Levels of Automation (2000, IEEE SMC)
Shneiderman, Human-Centered AI (2022); IJHCI (2020)

reading.text: Specify, in Horvitz's expected-utility terms, the interruption policy for a coding agent that is 80% confident it should refactor an adjacent file the user did not mention.

cards.back: Act when the expected utility of acting exceeds that of not acting, accounting for uncertainty about the user's goal and the cost of interrupting them.
Automation level applies per stage — information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, action implementation — not to the system as a whole.
Human control and automation are two independent axes, not endpoints of one slider. High-high is achievable and is the target quadrant.
An approval step the reviewer cannot meaningfully evaluate. It looks like control and functions as liability transfer.

cards.front: What should approval gates scale with?
cards.back: Reversibility and stakes. Cheap-to-undo actions should proceed; costly or irreversible ones should stop and ask.

quiz.question: Under Horvitz's principles, when should a confident agent still ask?
options: When the cost of being wrong is high relative to the cost of interrupting
Never — confidence is the only relevant variable
quiz.why: The rule is expected utility, not a confidence threshold. High confidence in a catastrophic, irreversible action can still fail the test.

quiz.question: A product shows a 12-step agent plan and an Approve button. Users approve in two seconds. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: The gate exists but the reviewer cannot actually assess the plan in the time and form given. It performs oversight without providing it.

quiz.question: What does Shneiderman's HCAI framework reject?
options: That automation can ever be safe
That human control and automation trade off against each other along one dimension
quiz.why: He reframes them as two axes, which makes the high-control-and-high-automation quadrant a design target rather than a contradiction.

lessons.title: Trust, Reliance, Automation Bias, and Explanation

items: Define calibrated trust and appropriate reliance
Explain why explanations can make things worse
Choose the right metric for a human-AI system

reading.text: This is the most consequential chapter in the book for anyone shipping an AI feature, because it contains the results that contradict the intuitive design moves. Explanations do not reliably help. More trust is not the goal. Adding a human does not automatically make a system safer.
Calibration, not confidence

Trust in automation (Lee & See, Human Factors, 2004) is the field's anchor paper. The goal is not maximal trust but calibrated trust, in which reliance tracks actual reliability. The three failure modes are misuse (overreliance), disuse (underreliance on a system that would have helped), and abuse (designers exploiting user trust).

Reframing the objective from trust to calibration changes what you build. If more trust is the goal, every design move points one way — reassurance, polish, confident phrasing. If calibration is the goal, the system sometimes needs to reduce trust: to say it is unsure, to show where it fails, to make its errors easy to find. Those are opposite designs, and most products are built as though the first were the aim.

Disuse deserves as much attention as misuse, and gets far less. A system ignored because it once embarrassed someone is a wasted capability, and the remedy is not more persuasion but a better account of when it can be relied on.

Automation bias and complacency (Parasuraman & Manzey, Human Factors, 2010): people favour automated cues and monitor less as reliability rises. It is worst when reliability is high but imperfect — exactly the LLM regime.

The shape of that finding is the important part. Low reliability keeps people checking, because they have learned they must. Perfect reliability makes checking pointless. High-but-imperfect suppresses monitoring while leaving errors that still matter — which is the single most dangerous operating point, and the one current models occupy.
Reliance is contextual, not a personality

Algorithm aversion (Dietvorst, Simmons & Massey, 2015): people abandon algorithms after seeing them err, even when the algorithm outperforms humans — an effect mitigated by giving users slight control over the output (Dietvorst 2018). The opposite pole is algorithm appreciation (Logg, Minson & Moore, 2019).

Those two literatures look contradictory and are not. Reliance depends on the task, the framing, the visibility of errors and how much agency the person retains — so the useful question is never "do people trust algorithms?" but "under what conditions, for this task, do they rely appropriately?" The Dietvorst mitigation is especially practical: letting someone adjust the output even slightly restores willingness to use it, at almost no cost to accuracy.

Overreliance countermeasures: cognitive forcing functions (Buçinca, Malaya & Gajos, CSCW 2021) reduce overreliance — and users dislike them. Microsoft's overreliance research programme (Passi & Vorvoreanu, 2022) catalogues the mitigation evidence.

A cognitive forcing function makes the person engage deliberately before they can accept the machine's answer — committing to their own answer first, or having the recommendation withheld until they have looked at the evidence. It works, and it is unpopular, which makes deployment an incentive problem rather than a solved interface problem: the intervention that improves decisions makes the product feel worse.
Explanation, and its sobering results

XAI meets HCI: technical methods such as LIME (Ribeiro et al., KDD 2016) and SHAP, alongside the attention-is-not-explanation debates — measured against human outcomes rather than mathematical fidelity.

The sobering results are the ones to remember. Explanations often increase unwarranted trust — a placebo effect of explanation (Eiband et al., CHI EA 2019), where the presence of a justification raises acceptance whether or not the justification is informative. Bansal et al. (CHI 2021) found explanations increased acceptance of wrong recommendations, which is the precise opposite of what they were added to do.

Miller's "Explanation in AI: Insights from the Social Sciences" (Artificial Intelligence, 2019) explains why the naive approach misfires. Human explanations are contrastive — people want to know why this rather than that; selective — a few relevant causes, not a complete causal account; and social — shaped for the recipient. A feature-importance chart is none of those things, which is why it satisfies the engineer and not the user.

Liao, Gruen & Miller's XAI Question Bank (CHI 2020) turns the problem the right way round: start from the questions users actually ask, and treat explanation as a user-needs problem rather than a model-introspection problem.
When does the team beat the parts?

Human-AI team performance (Bansal et al., AAAI 2019; CHI 2021): complementary performance — the team beating its best member — is rare, and it requires an accurate mental model of when the AI errs, not knowledge of its overall accuracy.

That distinction is the practical core. Being told a system is 90% accurate tells you nothing about which 10% to check; being told it fails on long documents, or on recent events, or on numerical reasoning, tells you where to look. Global accuracy supports a decision about whether to adopt; a model of the error distribution supports the decision you make on every individual output.

Kocielnik et al., "Will You Accept an Imperfect AI?" (CHI 2019), adds the timing: expectation setting before first use shifts acceptance, and shapes whether the first failure reads as a known limitation or a betrayal.

Uncertainty communication: verbalised confidence in LLMs is miscalibrated; quantile dotplots and frequency framings outperform percentages; and selective friction — friction applied only when stakes multiplied by uncertainty is high — is the active design direction.
Design guidelines, each tied to evidence

items: Set expectations before first use (Kocielnik et al. 2019)
Show when and why it errs, not merely that it can (Bansal et al. 2021)
Scale friction to stakes and reversibility (Buçinca; Horvitz)
Prefer contrastive, on-demand explanations (Miller; Liao)
Measure reliance appropriateness — accept-when-right minus accept-when-wrong — never raw acceptance rate

reading.text: That last line is the one to take into any product review. Raw acceptance rate rewards a system users trust indiscriminately, which is precisely the failure mode this chapter is about. The difference between accepting correct output and accepting incorrect output is the only number that distinguishes a useful assistant from a persuasive one.

items: Lee & See, Trust in Automation (2004, Human Factors, DOI 10.1518/hfes.46.1.50_30392)
Parasuraman & Manzey, complacency and bias (2010, Human Factors)
Dietvorst, Simmons & Massey (2015, JEP: General); Dietvorst (2018)
Logg, Minson & Moore, algorithm appreciation (2019)
Buçinca, Malaya & Gajos, To Trust or to Think (CSCW 2021, DOI 10.1145/3449287)
Ribeiro et al., LIME (KDD 2016)
Eiband et al. (CHI EA 2019)
Bansal et al., Does the Whole Exceed Its Parts? (CHI 2021)
Miller, Explanation in AI (2019, Artificial Intelligence)
Liao, Gruen & Miller, XAI Question Bank (CHI 2020)
Kocielnik et al., Will You Accept an Imperfect AI? (CHI 2019)

reading.text: Design the reliance dashboard for an AI radiology assistant. What does the hospital see about calibration that the radiologist does not, and vice versa?

cards.back: Trust that tracks actual reliability, so reliance rises where the system is reliable and falls where it is not. The goal is calibration, not maximum trust.
Misuse is overreliance; disuse is underreliance on a system that would help; abuse is designers exploiting user trust.
When reliability is high but imperfect. High reliability suppresses monitoring precisely where the remaining errors still matter.
Explanations increase trust and acceptance whether or not they are informative — including acceptance of wrong recommendations.
An accurate mental model of when the AI errs. Knowing its overall accuracy is not enough to beat the better member alone.
Accept-when-right minus accept-when-wrong. Raw acceptance rate rewards a system users trust indiscriminately.
An interface intervention that compels deliberate engagement before accepting AI output. It reduces overreliance, and users dislike it.
Contrastive (why this rather than that), selective (a few relevant causes, not all), and social (tailored to the recipient).

quiz.question: A product reports that 82% of AI suggestions are accepted. Why is this the wrong headline metric?
options: It should be measured per session
It cannot distinguish accepting correct suggestions from accepting wrong ones
quiz.why: Appropriate reliance is accept-when-right minus accept-when-wrong. A system users accept indiscriminately scores highly on raw acceptance and is dangerous.

quiz.question: Adding explanations to an AI recommender raised user agreement with wrong recommendations. What is this?
options: The placebo effect of explanation — explanation increases trust regardless of informativeness
quiz.why: The mere presence of an explanation signals competence. Bansal et al. and Eiband et al. both documented explanations increasing acceptance without improving discrimination.

quiz.question: Which condition produces the worst automation bias?
quiz.why: Low reliability keeps people checking and perfection makes checking pointless. High-but-imperfect suppresses monitoring while leaving errors that matter — the LLM regime.

quiz.question: Cognitive forcing functions reduce overreliance but face what obstacle?
options: Users dislike them, creating an incentive conflict with engagement metrics
quiz.why: Buçinca et al. found the intervention works and is unpopular. That makes deployment an incentive-design problem rather than a solved interface problem.

items: Distinguish adaptive from adaptable interfaces
State the cost adaptivity imposes
Apply contextual integrity to LLM memory

reading.text: Personalisation is the design move that looks obviously good and frequently is not. This chapter is mostly about the costs, because the benefits are the part everybody already believes in.
Adaptive versus adaptable

Adaptive means the system changes itself; adaptable means the user changes it. The classic cost is that adaptive interfaces break spatial memory and predictability — Findlater & McGrenere's split-menu studies (CHI 2004–08) found adaptivity helps only when prediction accuracy is high and layout stability is preserved.

The mechanism behind that cost is chapter 3's material. Experienced users locate items by remembered position rather than by reading labels, which is fast and nearly effortless. An interface that reorders itself invalidates that memory on every visit, so it taxes exactly the users who had become efficient — and it does so silently, since a menu that has quietly rearranged looks the same as one that has not.

The split menu is the design that survives the finding: a small adaptive section for frequent items sits above a stable section that never moves. The user's spatial memory of the main list stays intact, and the adaptation gets a bounded region to work in.

Recommender systems as HCI: GroupLens (Resnick et al., CSCW 1994); explanations for recommendations (Herlocker et al., CSCW 2000); and serendipity and diversity as goals that compete with raw accuracy.

The accuracy-versus-diversity tension is the interesting one. A recommender optimised purely for predicted rating converges on the safe and the similar, which scores well and serves the user poorly — nobody wants a system that only ever offers what they already know they like. Diversity and serendipity are not softness; they are corrections for an objective function that measures the wrong thing.

Filter bubbles were theorised by Pariser (2011) but have proved empirically weaker than feared in several large studies, with results that are platform-dependent. Engagement-optimisation critiques rest on firmer ground.
Memory, and the right privacy lens

LLM-era personalisation: persistent memory raises consent and legibility questions — what does it remember, can I see and edit it, does it leak across contexts? Memory UIs offering view, edit and delete are becoming a standard pattern, and contextual integrity (Nissenbaum) is the right privacy lens.

Contextual integrity is the concept that makes the problem tractable. It holds that privacy is not secrecy but appropriate flow: information shared in one context carries norms about where it may travel, and a violation occurs when it moves somewhere those norms did not sanction — even if nothing was disclosed to an outsider and no security boundary was crossed.

Apply that to an assistant with persistent memory and the failure becomes obvious. A medical detail mentioned in one conversation, surfaced during a work task, has not leaked in any technical sense. It has moved between contexts the user kept separate, which is exactly the harm the framework names — and it is why the remedy is legibility and control over what is retained rather than stronger encryption.

items: Findlater & McGrenere, split-menu studies (CHI 2004–08)
Resnick et al., GroupLens (CSCW 1994)
Herlocker et al., explanations for recommendations (CSCW 2000)
Pariser, The Filter Bubble (2011)
Nissenbaum, contextual integrity
Mireshghallah et al., Can LLMs Keep a Secret? (ICLR 2024)

cards.back: Adaptive: the system changes itself. Adaptable: the user changes it. Adaptable preserves predictability; adaptive risks breaking spatial memory.
Only when prediction accuracy is high and layout stability is preserved — otherwise the cost to spatial memory outweighs the saved effort.
Nissenbaum's framing: privacy is appropriate information flow relative to context norms, not secrecy. Cross-context leakage is a violation even without a breach.
Let users view, edit and delete what the system has remembered about them. Legibility and control are the design response to persistent memory.

quiz.question: A menu reorders itself to put your frequent items first, and users get slower. Why?
options: Reordering destroys spatial memory, which was doing more work than the shortened travel saved
quiz.why: Users locate familiar items by remembered position. Adaptive reordering invalidates that memory on every visit, which is why split menus keep the stable section intact.

quiz.question: An assistant mentions a user's medical detail from a months-old chat during a work task. Which framework names the violation?
options: Contextual integrity — appropriate flow relative to context norms
quiz.why: Nothing was disclosed to an outsider, so a secrecy model sees no problem. Contextual integrity captures why moving information across contexts is itself the harm.

items: Apply creativity-support-tool criteria
Understand ownership and homogenisation effects
Explain why human plus AI can underperform AI alone

reading.text: Two literatures meet in this chapter: what makes a tool support creative work, and what happens to decisions when a machine advises them. They are grouped because both turn on the same question — what the human contributes once the machine can produce a plausible answer.
Creativity support
Creativity support tools: Shneiderman's criteria (CACM 2007) and Resnick et al.'s design principles (2005) — low floor, high ceiling, wide walls.

The three-part formulation is more demanding than it sounds. A low floor means a beginner can start immediately. A high ceiling means an expert is not eventually constrained by the tool. Wide walls means the tool supports many different kinds of outcome rather than steering everyone toward the same one. Most tools achieve two: easy and shallow, or powerful and forbidding, or easy and powerful but opinionated about what you should make.

Co-creation empirics: the CoAuthor dataset (Lee, Liang & Yang, CHI 2022) captured writer-LLM interaction traces; Gero et al.'s Sparks explored science writing; and image-generation studies find that prompt iteration is itself the creative act.
Ownership and homogenisation

Perceived ownership drops as AI contribution grows. Doshi & Hauser (Science Advances, 2024) found individual creativity rises while collective diversity falls — many creators drawing on one model converge.

That result is worth sitting with, because the two halves point in opposite directions and both are real. Each individual writer produces better work with assistance. Across writers, the works resemble each other more than they would have. So a change that is an improvement at every individual desk is a loss at the level of the field — and no participant experiences the loss, which is what makes it hard to resist.

The ownership finding has a practical edge for anyone building creative tools. If heavier assistance reduces the sense that the work is yours, it also reduces willingness to stand behind it, to defend it, and to care about it — which are the things that make creative work worth doing at all.
High-stakes decisions

AI-assisted decisions in high stakes: Cai et al. (CSCW 2019) on pathologists' needs when onboarding an imperfect classifier; Green & Chen (CSCW 2019) on risk assessments, where human plus AI performed worse than AI alone because reliance was miscalibrated.

The Green and Chen result is the one that should unsettle anyone who treats human oversight as a safety guarantee. Adding a human did not add a check; it added a source of miscalibrated overrides — correct outputs rejected, incorrect ones accepted — and the combined system underperformed the model on its own.

The policy implication is to evaluate the sociotechnical system rather than the model. Whether a human in the loop helps is an empirical property of the combination, not something guaranteed by the arrangement.

Cai et al. supply the constructive counterpart: clinicians asked not for accuracy figures but for a sense of the model's character — what it tends to get wrong, what it is like as a colleague. That is the same requirement chapter 29 identified as the precondition for complementary performance, arriving from practitioners rather than from experiments.

items: Shneiderman, creativity support tools (CACM 2007)
Resnick et al., design principles for tools to support creative exploration (2005)
Lee, Liang & Yang, CoAuthor (CHI 2022)
Gero et al., Sparks
Doshi & Hauser (2024, Science Advances)
Cai et al., 'Hello AI' (CSCW 2019)
Green & Chen (CSCW 2019)

reading.text: Run the same illustration brief three times: unaided, with image-model assistance, and with an LLM acting as art director only. Journal ownership feeling, diversity of outcomes and time; compare with a peer.

cards.front: Low floor, high ceiling, wide walls
cards.back: Easy to start, capable of sophisticated work, and supportive of many different kinds of outcome.
Individual creative output improves with AI assistance while collective diversity declines, because many creators draw from the same model.

cards.front: Why can human + AI be worse than AI alone?
cards.back: Because miscalibrated reliance lets the human override correct outputs and accept incorrect ones — documented by Green & Chen in risk assessment.

cards.front: What happens to perceived ownership as AI contribution rises?
cards.back: It drops — which matters for authorship, motivation and whether people are willing to stand behind the work.

quiz.question: What is the policy implication of "human + AI performed worse than AI alone"?
options: Remove the human from the loop
Evaluate the sociotechnical system rather than the model, because adding a human is not automatically a safeguard
quiz.why: The finding refutes the assumption that human oversight can only help. Whether it helps is an empirical property of the combined system.

quiz.question: Doshi & Hauser found which pattern in AI-assisted creative work?
options: Both individual and collective creativity rose
Individual creativity rose while collective diversity fell
quiz.why: Each writer produced better work, and the works resembled each other more — a gain at the individual level that is a loss at the population level.
